cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Bahasa Indonesia at level B2 — leading an exchange programme in Jakarta: baku Indonesian and EYD, formal letters, negotiation, the media, regional speech and online slang, literature and pantun, law, speeches, and the UKBI.

product.title: Indonesian 101 - B2
product.description: The closing volume of the Indonesian 101 series: twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from B1 to a confident B2 in Bahasa Indonesia. Every unit has two dialogues, one in the register of the ministry, the boardroom or the stage and one in the register of the lunch table, the phone call or the group chat, each with a word-for-word translation, grammar notes, vocabulary with pronunciation, four keyed exercises and a wave review of earlier units. At this level Indonesian is about choosing a register: baku spelling and word forms by KBBI and EYD, nominalisation and the effective sentence, the formal letter and the proposal, long sentences without the di mana calque, hedging and negotiation, opinion writing, legal and report language, the sambutan, criticism without offence, respectful talk across faiths, and the UKBI proficiency test, alongside Betawi, Javanese, Batak, Makassar and Papuan speech, online slang and acronyms, literature and the pantun. The story follows Sarah as she directs Program Jembatan in Jakarta: a budget deal over dinner, an MoU, the first student cohort flown to Australia, baby Kinan, the UKBI and the closing speech. Includes a B1 review, a B2 grammar and usage summary and a map of registers.

blocks.text: At A1 Indonesian got you through the day. At A2 it let you run a life. At B1 you took part: the meeting, the opinion, the soft no. **B2 is the level at which you choose.** Every sentence you now produce comes with a decision attached: *baku* or everyday, *saya* or *aku* or *gue*, *tidak* or *nggak*, a letter that opens with *Dengan hormat* or a message that opens with *Pak, maaf mengganggu*. Indonesians make that choice dozens of times a day without noticing. This book teaches you to make it on purpose first, and then, with enough practice, without noticing either.

The formal side has a referee, and it is written down. The *KBBI*, the official dictionary, and the *EYD*, the spelling rules, have decided that it is *mengubah* and not *merubah*, *praktik* and not *praktek*, *izin* and not *ijin* (Unit 1). Educated Indonesians get these wrong in writing every day, and a ministry official with a red pen notices every one. So you learn the rules properly. Then you learn the half no dictionary teaches: **when to bend them**. A message to a colleague in flawless *baku* sounds cold; a speech in Jakarta slang sounds like a joke. Knowing the rule is B2. Knowing when the rule is not the point is B2 as well.

Here is the honest part. The grammar is nearly finished; what remains is craft. Unit 2 teaches the **effective sentence** (*kalimat efektif*): the nouns that give a report its weight (*pelaksanaan, peningkatan*) and the spare parts an editor cuts (*para peserta-peserta*, *sangat … sekali*, the much-abused *daripada*). Unit 3 is the **formal letter**, formula by formula. Unit 4 builds long sentences without the English calques *di mana* and *yang mana*. Unit 5 is **negotiation**, where *Akan kami pelajari dulu* usually means no and *alangkah baiknya* is really an instruction. Units 11 and 12 take on **legal and report language** (*sebagaimana dimaksud, terhitung sejak, meningkat sebesar*), and Unit 13 the **sambutan**, the speech that opens every Indonesian event and whose edges matter more than its middle.

Then there is everything the formal register leaves out. Unit 7 is **regional Indonesian**: Betawi *kagak* and *udeh*, Javanese *nggih* and *monggo*, Batak *kau* and *bah*, Makassar *-mi* and *-ji*, Papuan *sa* and *ko*. Unit 8 is **online Indonesian**: *mager, gabut, otw, gpp*, and the acronyms (*Jabodetabek, Pemda, ASN*) that fill every official message. Unit 6 reads a newspaper, Unit 9 reads Chairil Anwar and Pramoedya and writes a *pantun*, Unit 14 gets the jokes, and Unit 15 finally tells *kesal* from *jengkel* from *dongkol*.

The story continues from B1. It is 2029, and Sarah is back in Jakarta, where it all began, as director of **Program Jembatan**, an Australia–Indonesia education exchange with an office in Kuningan. Her deputy **Fajar**, a Betawi from Condet, speaks the fastest Jakarta slang in the building. **Yoga**, the intern from Sumberwangi, is now a junior staffer. **Pak Hendra**, her very first boss, is the director she reports to. **Ibu Maria Simanjuntak**, a Batak official at the ministry, is very formal, very direct and armed with a red pen. **Mbak Dewi** is the education reporter who becomes a friend, and **Dr. Lestari**, now teaching in Jakarta, is still the one who checks the drafts. Rina and Andi, married at the end of B1, are expecting their first child.

Over twenty units the programme writes to the ministry (Unit 3), agrees a budget over grilled fish (Unit 5), gets into the paper (Unit 6), signs an MoU (Unit 11), faces the board (Unit 12) and sends its first forty students to Australia with a sambutan (Unit 13). In June Rina and Andi's daughter **Kinan** is born, and Sarah writes her a pantun (Unit 9). In November Sarah sits the **UKBI**, the official Indonesian proficiency test (Unit 18). And on 15 December 2029 she gives the closing speech of the programme's first year, answers the press, and ends the day on Rina's sofa (Unit 20), which is also where this series ends.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Give each unit two sittings of about 45 minutes. At B2 the dialogues are longer in feel than in lines: a letter or a contract clause needs to be read twice before it gives up its structure.
Read both dialogues **out loud**. The formal one is a model to copy; the casual one is a model to recognise. The next chapter says more about the difference.
Keep *KBBI Daring*, the free online edition of the dictionary, open while you work. Looking a word up to check its *baku* form is the habit this book is trying to build.
Make sure the B1 review at the end of this front matter holds no surprises. If three or more of its tables look unfamiliar, go back to B1 first.
Keep the answer key covered until you have finished a whole exercise. Being wrong and finding out why is still the fastest way to learn.

blocks.text: *Selamat belajar*, and welcome back to Jakarta.

The shape is the same as in B1. Each unit is built to be finished in two sittings of about 45 minutes, and every part has a job. What has changed is the distance between the two dialogues: at B2 one of them is often a letter, a contract or a speech, and the other a lunch, a phone call or a family dinner. Read them as a pair; the gap between them is the lesson.

items: **Two dialogues.** The first runs to 13–15 lines and is usually the public scene: a meeting, a ministry, an interview, a stage. The second, 9–11 lines, moves to a different place and usually a different register. Under every line: the natural English, then the word-for-word English.
**Notes.** Six after each dialogue: the words, forms and customs in those lines that would have quietly confused you.
**Grammar boxes.** Three per unit, two after the first dialogue and one after the second, each with a table you can keep.
**Two extra sections.** Word fields, document templates, formulas and culture that the dialogues only touch on.
**Wave review.** Five lines from two units back, to rebuild from memory.
**Vocabulary.** Every new word, in the order it appears, with the Say it column and the English.

**Exercises and answer key.** Four sets of six items: a translation, a gap fill, a transformation (make it *baku*, make it effective, make it formal, say it the Jakarta way) and a word-order puzzle. That is 480 items across the book.

blocks.title: Two kinds of model line
items: **Baku lines are models to copy.** When Ibu Maria, Pak Ilham the museum guide or the lawyer Bu Ratih speaks, and whenever a letter, clause or speech is quoted, the Indonesian is standard and checked against KBBI and EYD. Lift these sentences whole into your own writing: they will not come back with red ink on them.

**Spoken lines are models to recognise.** Fajar's *gue, kagak, udeh*, Yoga's *mager* and *gabut*, Ani's *-mi* and Nando's *sa* and *ko* are exactly what you will hear, and the notes always give the standard form beside them. Understand them all; use them only once someone has used them with you (Unit 7), and never in writing that matters.

**Neutral lines are the ones to live in.** Sarah, most of the time, speaks the polite everyday Indonesian of an educated professional: *saya*, *Bapak* and *Ibu*, *tidak* on paper and *nggak* over lunch. If you are unsure which register to use, use hers.

blocks.title: The word-for-word line
items: Hyphens join what is **one word** in Indonesian but several in English: *dilampirkan* → "is-attached", *laporannya* → "report-the", *kiranya* → "it-is-hoped", *keterlambatan* → "lateness" needs none.

Particles with no English equivalent stay in square brackets: *[kan] [kok] [sih] [dong] [deh] [lho] [ya] [nih] [tuh] [-lah] [-kah] [pun]*, and the regional ones too: *[to] [bah] [-mi] [-ji] [e] [mah]*.
The line is deliberately ungrammatical English. At B2 its main job is to show you how a long formal sentence is built, which is the first step to building one yourself.

blocks.title: The Say it column
items: Syllables are separated by hyphens and the **stressed syllable is in CAPITALS**: *kesepakatan* kuh-suh-pa-KA-tan, *sambutan* sam-BU-tan.
**uh** is the schwa, the vowel of "about": *menerapkan* muh-nuh-RAP-kan. When the second-last syllable has a schwa, the stress slides to the last one: *empat* uhm-PAT.
**É** is the *e* of "bed" in a stressed syllable, **é** in an unstressed one: *enak* É-nak, *efektif* é-FÉK-tif.
Everything else is spelled as written: *c* is always "ch", *ng* as in "singer", *ny* as in "canyon", *kh* as in Scottish "loch" (though many speakers say plain *k*).

blocks.text: **The wave.** The third section of every unit is a table of five lines from the unit two before it, English on the left, Indonesian on the right. Cover the right-hand column and rebuild each sentence aloud. Units 1 and 2 reach back to the last two units of B1: Rina's wedding and the festival in Sumberwangi.

blocks.title: Two symbols used throughout
items: ⚠️ — a mistake nearly every foreign learner makes here, or one that many Indonesians make in writing too. At B2 a lot of these are the errors the UKBI tests (Unit 18).
💬 — the everyday spoken form, next to the written one it replaces. At B2 the point is not to avoid it but to know exactly when it belongs.

blocks.text: **A realistic pace:** two units a week, one wave review each time, and one older unit re-read aloud at the weekend. That is ten weeks to the end of the book and of the series. At this level slower and steadier really does work better: write something every week, even a short paragraph, and check it against KBBI.

back.title: B2 grammar and usage at a glance

blocks.text: No long explanations here: everything was explained in its unit. This is the map for revision, the page to open before you send an important email, and, if you sit the UKBI, the list to read the night before.
1. Baku spelling and word forms (Units 1, 18)
⚠️ *di-* the prefix is joined, *di* the preposition is separate: *dikirim* but *di kementerian*; *keluar* but *ke luar negeri*. When in doubt, KBBI Daring decides.
2. Nominalisation (Unit 2)
The nouns give a report its weight; too many of them make it unreadable. ⚠️ An empty verb plus a noun is always worse than the verb: *melakukan pelaksanaan* → *melaksanakan*.
3. The effective sentence: cut the spare parts (Units 2, 18)
*Daripada* has two jobs only: "than" (*lebih baik daripada versi lama*) and "rather than" (*Daripada menunggu, lebih baik kita mulai*). It is never "of".
4. The sentence with no subject (Unit 18)

head: Wrong
Right
rows: *Rapat itu membahas anggaran.* / *Dalam rapat itu dibahas anggaran.*

blocks.text: The rule: a preposition in front of the subject turns it into an adverbial, and the sentence is left without one. Remove the preposition, or make the verb passive.
5. The official letter (Unit 3)

head: Part
Formula
English
rows: This is the content of our letter.
*Atas perhatian dan kerja sama Bapak/Ibu, kami ucapkan terima kasih.*
Thank you for your attention and cooperation.

blocks.text: Compounds stay apart with one affix and join with two: *tanda tangan*, *bertanda tangan*, *menandatangani*; *tindak lanjut*, *menindaklanjuti*; *beri tahu*, *memberi tahu*, *memberitahukan*.
6. Long sentences without calques (Unit 4)

head: Calque (avoid)
Standard
English
rows: the schools where our teachers teach
the report which has been sent

blocks.text: Opening phrases borrow the subject of the main clause, so it must be the same person: *Setelah membaca laporan itu, Ibu Maria menelepon kami. Dengan mempertimbangkan hasil survei, kami merekomendasikan… Berdasarkan data tahun lalu, …*
7. Hedging and negotiating (Unit 5)
8. Building an argument (Units 6, 19)

head: Move
Markers
rows: *Tidak dapat dimungkiri bahwa…, Harus diakui bahwa…, Memang benar…, namun…*
*Di satu sisi… di sisi lain…, Sementara itu…, Sebaliknya…*
*Selain itu…, Di samping itu…, Lebih lanjut…*
*Oleh sebab itu…, Dengan demikian…, Pada akhirnya…*

blocks.text: In writing, the spoken openers move up a register: *Tapi* → *Namun*, *Jadi* → *Oleh karena itu*, *Makanya* → *Itulah sebabnya*, *Soalnya* → *Hal itu disebabkan oleh*, *Terus* → *Kemudian*. One paragraph, one idea, stated in its *kalimat utama*.
9. Legal and bureaucratic language (Unit 11)

The modal verbs of law are exact: *wajib* is an obligation, *harus* a requirement, *dapat* a permission, *berhak* a right and *dilarang* a prohibition. Numbers are written twice: *60 (enam puluh) hari*.
10. Numbers and trends (Unit 12)

*meningkat sebesar 35 persen* is "by"; *meningkat menjadi 1.250* is "to"; *dibandingkan dengan tahun lalu* is "compared with". ⚠️ The comma is the decimal point and the point separates thousands: *4,6* is 4.6, *1.250* is 1,250, *Rp4,2 miliar* is Rp4.2 billion.
11. The sambutan (Unit 13)

head: Step
Formula
rows: *Yang terhormat…, yang saya hormati…, Bapak dan Ibu sekalian…*
*Selamat pagi dan salam sejahtera bagi kita semua.* (or a religious greeting)
*Puji syukur kita panjatkan ke hadirat Tuhan Yang Maha Esa…*
*Demikian yang dapat saya sampaikan. Mohon maaf apabila ada kata-kata yang kurang berkenan.*

blocks.text: The MC's formulas run the rest of the event: *Acara selanjutnya adalah…, Hadirin dimohon berdiri, …waktu dan tempat kami persilakan* (Units 13, 20). Your own team or students are *yang saya banggakan*.

blocks.text: Name the cause with *membuat* (formal) or *bikin* (casual): *Kabar itu membuat saya lega. Kinan bikin aku gemas.*

Softened

Next time it might be better to…

blocks.text: Acknowledge first, then turn: *Saya pahami… Namun, …*; *Memang benar…, hanya saja…*. Cushion written criticism with *Mohon maaf sebelumnya*, and apologise at the level of the relationship: *Kami mohon maaf atas…* in a letter, *Maaf, ya, saya yang lupa* to a colleague.

*Selamat pagi dan salam sejahtera bagi kita semua.*

items: **Also in B2:** regional Indonesian (Unit 7) and online slang and acronyms (Unit 8), both on the next page; talking about literature, old spelling and writing a *pantun* (Unit 9); the history of the national language and the formal narrative past with *telah, menjelang, konon, hingga kini* (Unit 10); jokes, *plesetan* and *pantun jenaka* (Unit 14); and the UKBI, its five sections and seven bands, from *Terbatas* to *Istimewa* (Unit 18).

blocks.text: Indonesian does not have two registers, formal and informal. It has a ladder, and every speaker moves up and down it through the day, as Sarah does in Unit 20: *yang terhormat* on the stage in the morning, *menurut hemat saya* to the press, *Itu kemajuan juga, Pak* to Pak Hendra and *capek banget, Rin* on the sofa at night. Below, the same message on five rungs.
"The report has been sent."

blocks.title: Echo, don't lead
items: Use a regional or slang form only after someone has used it with you, and only in the setting where they used it. Sarah's *enak kali* works at Pak Tigor's table; *kau* to Ibu Maria at the ministry would not.
*Gue* and *lo* are for friends and colleagues of your own age. In a meeting or with an elder they sound cheeky.
Javanese *nggih* and *monggo* to an older Javanese person, and *horas* to a Batak host, read as respect, not mimicry.
Never copy an accent for a laugh, however kindly meant.
Chat shorthand (*yg, dgn, gpp, otw*) belongs in chats. An email to a ministry is written in full, in *baku*, with *Yth.* at the top.

blocks.text: If you have really worked through these twenty units, and the sixty before them, you have finished the **Indonesian 101 series, from A1 to B2**. You can write a letter that a ministry official will not send back, cut a report down to effective sentences, negotiate without saying *tidak*, read a contract clause and explain it in plain words, give a sambutan in the right order, follow an opinion piece and argue with it, and hear where in the archipelago a speaker grew up. Above all, you can choose your register, and change it when the room changes. That is a solid, independent B2.

**C1** is the level at which the choosing stops being work. You read a *Kompas* or *Tempo* editorial for the argument rather than the words. You finish a novel without a dictionary on the table. You follow a podcast at full speed, with its jokes, its interruptions and its particles. You write a column that an editor corrects for style, not for grammar. And you sit the UKBI again, aiming for *Sangat Unggul*. No book gets you there on its own; habits do.
Four habits that work from here:

items: **Read one opinion column a day.** *Kompas*, *Tempo* or any national daily's *rubrik opini*. Afterwards, say its argument out loud in two sentences, using the moves of Unit 6: what it concedes, what it counters, what it concludes.
**Read one novel a season.** Start with Andrea Hirata's *Laskar Pelangi*, then Pramoedya's *Bumi Manusia*, then Leila S. Chudori or Eka Kurniawan. Read for the story; the vocabulary comes with it.

**Listen to people talking to each other.** Talk radio such as RRI, current-affairs podcasts, long interviews. Not subtitled clips: real conversation at real speed, which is where C1 listening is built.

**Write every week and get corrected.** A letter, a summary, an essay of the kind in Unit 19. Check every word against *KBBI Daring*, then send it to a native reader and ask for red ink. Ibu Maria was right: the red pen is the fastest teacher there is.

blocks.text: And keep one thing from this book above all: the group chat. Reply, joke, send the sticker, get the *wkwk* back. That is the Indonesian nobody writes down, and it is how a language stops being a subject and becomes a life.

Sarah's story began in A1 with *Selamat pagi* in a Jakarta office, a new colleague called Rina and a head of department called Pak Hendra. It ends in B2 with Rina and Pak Hendra still beside her, a programme that will run for two more years, an Unggul on the UKBI, and Sarah on Rina's sofa, teaching Kinan the words she started with. *Karena aku udah pulang, Rin.* She came back, as she promised. We hope you will too: to Indonesia, to its people, and to the language that makes you at home there.
*Kalau ada sumur di ladang, / boleh kita menumpang mandi. / Kalau ada umur panjang, / boleh kita berjumpa lagi.*
*Terima kasih, sampai jumpa, dan selamat berbahasa Indonesia!*
